title.script: Welcome back, everyone! Tonight we hit a real turning point. You already know how to fit a model and get a score, but here's the tricky part: how do you turn that number into something another person can actually believe? Over the next hour, we'll run a couple of hands-on labs and work through some quick checks, all built on a dataset you can reproduce yourself. By the end, you'll be able to make a fair, honest claim about your models.

quiz-fair-claim.script: Here's a quick puzzle for you. Model A scores 0.91, Model B scores 0.86, and it's tempting to just say A wins by 0.05, right? But look closer — two things changed at once here: the model *and* the test data they were measured on. When two things change together, you can't tell which one caused the difference — that's what we call a confound. So the honest answer is that we can conclude nothing yet, until we test both models on the exact same split.

concept-question.script: Here's a habit that will save you so much confusion: before you write a single line of code, write your experiment as one sentence. Something like, "On the same data, split, and metric, does model B beat the baseline on F1?" That one sentence forces you to name three things — the one thing you're changing, the outcome you'll measure, and everything you're holding constant. If your sentence can't name all three, no amount of clever code will rescue the design.

concept-baseline.script: Here's a rule I want you to live by: every model you build must beat a baseline, the simplest credible rule that answers your question. Look what happens when our baseline just always predicts the majority class — it gets 71 percent accuracy, correct on 107 out of 150 rows. Sounds impressive, right? But it finds zero of the positive cases, so its recall and F1 are both flat zero. That high accuracy was just sitting there, free, without learning anything useful — so now you know exactly how much your real model has to earn.

quiz-baseline.script: Let's think carefully about this one. Your dataset is 72 percent class zero, so a lazy model that always guesses zero already scores 72 percent accuracy — but it never catches a single case of class one. Now your model hits 74 percent and catches only 5 percent of class one. So beating the baseline is nice, but a two-point gain that tiny needs uncertainty and the metric that actually matters for the cost of being wrong. Beating baseline is necessary, but never sufficient.

concept-control.script: Here's the golden rule of a fair experiment: change one thing, and freeze everything else. If you want to know whether SVM beats logistic regression, you keep the same data, the same split, the same scaling, and the same metric — then only the model changes, so any difference is genuinely down to the model. But if you swap the model and add new features and change the split and tune the threshold all at once, and the score goes up, you honestly can't say what caused it. That messy version might still help you ship a product, but it can never explain why it worked.

concept-same-split.script: Here's something that should make you a little nervous. Take the exact same model, the exact same data, and just change how you randomly split it into training and testing sets. Do that twenty times, and your F1 score bounces between 0.563 and 0.737 — a swing of 0.174, larger than many improvements people brag about in papers. So the fix is simple: create one split, save those indices, and hand the identical split to every model you're comparing. Never reroll until you get the number you like.

quiz-same-split.script: Here's a tricky one. Our KNN model used one random seed, and our SVM used a completely different one, and now SVM looks better by a tiny 0.04 in F1. But think about what those different seeds actually did — they shuffled the data differently, so each model was tested on a different set of rows. That gap could be pure luck, not real skill. Before you trust any winner, run both models on the exact same saved split, and freeze those evaluation rows so you only tune inside the training data.

concept-leakage.script: Here's one of the sneakiest traps in machine learning: leakage, where information from the future or from the answer itself slips into your training data. Watch what happens in our little experiment. An honest model scores about 81 percent accuracy, which is respectable. But when I secretly add a feature that's basically a copy of the answer, accuracy jumps to a perfect 100 percent. That perfect score isn't success, it's an alarm bell telling you something has leaked.

concept-pipeline.script: Here's a mistake that quietly ruins a lot of experiments. If you scale your entire dataset before cross-validation, the test rows secretly help calculate the means and standard deviations, so your model peeks at data it shouldn't see. The fix is to wrap your preprocessing and model together in a pipeline, so each fold learns its scaling from only its own training rows. Remember the order: split first, fit your transformations second, then apply them to the held-out rows. And this isn't just scaling — it covers imputation, PCA, and feature selection too.

quiz-leakage.script: Here's a subtle trap. Imagine you fill in all your missing values using the median of the entire dataset before you split for cross-validation. It feels harmless, right? But that full-data median secretly contains information from every fold you're about to validate on, so each held-out fold has quietly influenced its own preprocessing. Even if the score barely shifts, this is unfair by process — the fix is to put your imputer inside a pipeline so each training fold learns its own median.

concept-cv.script: Here's an honest way to test your model: instead of trusting one lucky split, you make five versions. Each time you train on four parts of your data and test on the one part left out, so every single row gets a turn being tested. Now, five isn't magic — what really matters is how you split. If your rows have classes, keep the proportions balanced; if they involve the same person or time order, keep them together so your test mirrors the real world you'll deploy in.

But that last fold dropped to 0.448, and the spread of plus or minus 0.112 tells the real story. That low fold isn't noise to delete — it's a signal that one group of data is much harder, and it's begging you to investigate why.

concept-confusion.script: Let's open up the score and read these four boxes carefully. We correctly rejected 97 cases and correctly flagged 27, but look at the mistakes: 16 positive cases slipped through as false negatives, and 10 times we raised a false alarm. Every fancy metric you'll ever hear is just a summary of these four numbers. And here's the key habit—always say which class you're calling "positive," because swapping it flips your precision and recall even when accuracy stays exactly the same. So which of these boxes does your own project fear the most?

concept-metrics.script: Here's something crucial: these four numbers all describe the same model, but they ask completely different questions. Accuracy tells us how often we got any label right, precision asks how trustworthy our positive predictions are, and recall asks how many of the real positives we actually caught. F1 blends precision and recall together, but it's not just a polite compromise. The real skill is deciding before you look which mistake hurts more, and if missing positives is costly, you lean on recall.

quiz-metrics.script: Here's the key idea: when missing a real positive is much more expensive than dealing with a false alarm, you want to prioritize recall, because recall tells you what fraction of the actual positives you actually caught. But here's the catch — you can cheat your way to high recall by flagging almost everything, so always report precision and the confusion matrix alongside it. The portable rule is simple: name your most expensive mistake first, then choose the metric that guards against it.

concept-threshold.script: Here's something really powerful: the model gives you a score, but you get to choose where to draw the line. Look what happens as we move that threshold. When we lower it to 0.30, we catch more of the real cases, so recall jumps up, but we also raise a lot of false alarms. Push it up to 0.70 and we're much more precise, but now we miss far more. And the beautiful part is you never retrain the model to do this — you're just picking the rule that fits what mistakes you can live with.

concept-cost-rule.script: Here's something crucial that often gets buried in machine learning projects. When you set a threshold, you're making a value judgment, and I want you to write down the cost of your mistakes before you ever look at the results. Say it plainly, something like "a false negative costs five times a false positive," and then decide who actually owns that statement. That five-to-one ratio I'm using is just for teaching, real weights come from domain experts, affected people, and sometimes the law. The model gives you probabilities, but the people decide what to do with them, so never hide that second decision behind the words "the AI chose."

quiz-threshold.script: Here's a great question to test your intuition. When you lower the threshold from 0.70 down to 0.30, you're basically lowering the bar that a case has to clear to be flagged as positive. So more cases sneak over that lower bar — which means you catch more true positives, but you also raise more false alarms. And here's the key insight: the model itself doesn't change at all. Its coefficients stay exactly the same; you've only adjusted the decision rule you apply on top of it.
